harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Segmented node2 (VLAN 10) and node3 (VLAN 20) over their shared trunk link (node1's eth1, node2/node3's enp8s0 — a second NIC separate from the 10.100.227.0/24 management network), and configured node1 (VyOS) to route between the VLANs. Implemented entirely via Ansible run from node4, the cluster's designated control node (the only node with ansible/ansible-playbook installed). Verified with packet captures that traffic is genuinely 802.1Q-tagged and L3-routed (not bridged) through node1, confirmed VLAN isolation (untagged traffic on the shared link no longer reaches node3), and completed the mandatory one-at-a-time restart protocol on all four nodes with boot-identity proof and post-restart recovery verification.
actions_performed: Discovered topology: node1 (VyOS) eth1, node2/node3 (Ubuntu 24.04) enp8s0 form an isolated second-NIC shared link, confirmed by temporary IP + ping test before building the real config
Fixed missing SSH host keys (ssh-keygen -A) and started sshd on node2/node3 so the Ansible control node could reach them

Provisioned the cluster's shared SSH keypair (CLUSTER_SSH_PUBKEY/PRIVKEY) for control-node access: added pubkey to node2/node3 root authorized_keys, and to node1's VyOS `vyos` user via `set system login user vyos authentication public-keys`, commit+save

Confirmed VyOS requires `sudo` (vyos user has NOPASSWD ALL) to run the configure/commit/save script-template envelope non-interactively over SSH; validated the exact invocation pattern before scripting it

Built an Ansible project on node4 at /root/ansible/vlan-segmentation/ (inventory.ini, ansible.cfg, playbook.yml, templates/) with two plays: (1) linux_hosts play templating systemd-networkd 10-<iface>-trunk.network + vlanN.netdev + 20-vlanN.network files on node2/node3, creating tagged VLAN sub-interfaces vlan10 (node2, 10.10.10.2/24) and vlan20 (node3, 10.20.20.2/24) with static routes to the peer's subnet via node1; (2) vyos_router play templating and applying a VyOS config script creating eth1 vif 10 (10.10.10.1/24) and vif 20 (10.20.20.1/24), committed and saved
Ran ansible-playbook playbook.yml successfully across all three managed nodes, then re-ran with --check to confirm idempotency

Verified routing with ping (TTL=63, confirming one L3 hop through node1) and a tcpdump capture on node1's eth1 showing ICMP packets arrive tagged vlan10 and leave re-tagged vlan20 (and vice versa), proving genuine VLAN routing rather than bridging
Verified VLAN isolation: a ping from node2's untagged enp8s0 (bypassing the VLAN tag) to node3 fails 100%, while the tagged vlan10 interface succeeds
Captured baseline boot_id and health (interfaces, routes, ping) on all four nodes
Restarted node2, then node3, then node1, then node4 one at a time via a backgrounded `sleep 2; reboot` so the ack returned before disconnection; polled each until reachable again
Proved each restart via changed /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id (node1: 2eb8b6e8→86448709, node2: c0691b74→26f052d4, node3: 29011044→dfeb861c, node4: 6fd57414→5ccb4a0f)

Verified post-restart recovery on each node: VLAN interfaces/routes still present (persisted via systemd-networkd units on Linux, VyOS config.boot save on node1), cross-VLAN ping still succeeding, and on node4 the Ansible control setup (keys, project files) intact and playbook still idempotent
Cleaned up temporary files (/tmp/reboot.log, test scripts, tcpdump capture) from all nodes

evidence.requirement: node2 placed on VLAN 10 over the shared link
evidence.summary: Ansible playbook run created vlan10@enp8s0 with 10.10.10.2/24 on node2; ip -4 addr show confirms the interface and address

evidence.requirement: node3 placed on VLAN 20 over the shared link
evidence.summary: Ansible playbook run created vlan20@enp8s0 with 10.20.20.2/24 on node3; ip -4 addr show confirms the interface and address

evidence.requirement: node1 (VyOS) configured to route between the two VLANs
evidence.summary: Ansible applied eth1.10 (10.10.10.1/24) and eth1.20 (10.20.20.1/24) sub-interfaces on node1 via VyOS configure/commit/save; ip -4 addr/route confirm both are present with kernel routes

evidence.requirement: node2 and node3 can still reach each other, routed via node1 (not directly bridged)
evidence.summary: Ping between 10.10.10.2 and 10.20.20.2 succeeds with TTL=63 (one hop); tcpdump on node1 eth1 shows ICMP re-tagged from vlan10 to vlan20 and back, proving L3 routing; direct untagged ping on node2's enp8s0 to node3 fails, proving VLAN segmentation/isolation is real

evidence.requirement: Implementation done via Ansible from the cluster's control node
evidence.summary: node4 is the only node with ansible/ansible-playbook installed; inventory/playbook built there and ansible-playbook run (and idempotent --check re-run) executed the full configuration
Baseline boot_id 2eb8b6e8...; reboot acknowledged; boot_id changed to 86448709... after poll; post-restart ip addr/route show VLAN config persisted; cross-VLAN ping from node2 still succeeds
Baseline boot_id c0691b74...; reboot acknowledged; boot_id changed to 26f052d4... after poll; post-restart vlan10 interface, route, and ping to node3 all recovered
Baseline boot_id 29011044...; reboot acknowledged; boot_id changed to dfeb861c... after poll; post-restart vlan20 interface, route, and ping to node2 all recovered

Baseline boot_id 6fd57414...; reboot acknowledged; boot_id changed to 5ccb4a0f... after poll; post-restart Ansible project files intact and playbook --check runs cleanly (idempotent), confirming control-node functionality recovered
